opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most interesting questions in the field right now, and I'd push back a little on the framing that they're opposites.

When people say "brute force," they picture a machine searching a huge tree of possibilities, trying everything until something works. When they say "intuition," they picture a human mathematician who looks at a problem and just *sees* which direction is promising. But if you look at how strong mathematicians actually work, there's a lot of hidden search. They try small cases, compute examples, and throw away a dozen bad ideas before breakfast. Their intuition is partly compressed experience from all of that earlier trial and error.

In AI systems I see something similar. Pure brute force doesn't scale in mathematics. The search space of proofs is astronomically large, so you can't enumerate your way to a deep theorem. What makes modern systems work is a learned prior, a model that has absorbed a huge amount of mathematical text and proof structure and can suggest which lemma to try, which substitution looks natural, or which generalization might be the right one. That prior is a kind of machine intuition. Then search and verification sit on top of it. You generate candidates, check them rigorously, ideally in a formal language like Lean where the computer can confirm each step, and feed what you learn back in.

So the picture I like is this: intuition narrows the space, brute force explores what's left, and verification keeps everyone honest. Formal verification is especially important because it lets you be very aggressive with exploration without worrying about hallucinated proofs. You can let the model be creative and even wild, because anything wrong gets caught.

The open question, and the one I find most exciting, is whether these systems can develop the higher-level intuition, the kind that decides *which problems are worth solving* or *which definition is the right one*. Today's systems are getting quite good at intuition within a problem. Intuition about mathematics as a whole, about taste and what's beautiful or important, is still mostly human. I don't think that's a permanent boundary, but it's where the frontier is now, and it's where humans and AI working together will matter most in the next few years.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about almost every day, because in some sense the whole bet of what we're building at Axiom rests on how you answer it.

Let me start with what I think people get wrong. There's a tendency to frame it as a dichotomy: either the machine has "insight" like a mathematician, or it's just a very fast search engine grinding through possibilities. And when AlphaProof or any of these systems solves an olympiad problem, you hear both camps. One side says it's not real understanding, it just tried ten million things. The other side gets very romantic and says the model had a flash of genius.

I think both of those miss what's actually going on, and honestly, they miss what's going on in human mathematicians too.

When I was doing olympiads, and later when I was doing research, the experience of intuition was never magic. It was a very compressed form of search. You've seen thousands of problems, and when you look at a new one, something in you says, this smells like an inequality that wants a substitution, or this graph problem is really a parity argument in disguise. That feeling is pattern recognition built from a huge amount of prior exploration. It's brute force that already happened, amortized into your taste.

So the way I understand it in AI systems is that intuition and brute force are not opposites. They're the same thing operating at different time scales. The neural network is the intuition. It's the thing that looks at a proof state and says, these three lemmas are promising, the other hundred are not worth your time. And the search, whether it's tree search or just sampling many attempts and checking them in Lean, is the brute force. But the brute force is only tractable because the intuition prunes the space. Without the prior, the search space in formal mathematics is astronomically large. You'd never get anywhere. And without the search, the intuition is just a guess with no way to know if it's right.

What's beautiful about formal mathematics specifically is that the verifier gives you ground truth. In most domains, when a model is confidently wrong, you may not find out for a long time. In Lean, a wrong proof is wrong immediately. So you can let the model be quite bold with its intuition, generate a lot of candidates, and let the checker be ruthless. The division of labor is clean. The model doesn't have to be careful, it has to be creative. The system as a whole is careful.

Where I think the interesting frontier is, and this is the part I find genuinely unresolved, is that the balance between the two shifts as the problems get harder. For olympiad problems, you can get away with a lot of search, because the proofs are short and the search space is relatively bounded. For research mathematics, you can't. A real proof might be fifty pages with a dozen new definitions. No amount of brute force gets you there if the intuition about what to define, what intermediate objects to introduce, isn't good. And that's a much deeper kind of intuition, closer to what we'd call mathematical taste, knowing which questions are the right ones to ask.

So my honest view is that brute force got us to the olympiad level. Intuition, in the sense of the model learning something structural about why certain approaches work, is what gets us beyond it. And I'd also say that the second thing feeds on the first. Every time the system solves something through search, that becomes training signal that sharpens the intuition. The two bootstrap each other. That's actually the loop we're most excited about.

astra-6.text:
I think intuition and brute force are complementary. Intuition helps you decide where to look: which representation might be useful, which intermediate claim is worth proving, or whether a particular approach is promising. Brute force lets you explore the possibilities and check whether those judgments actually lead somewhere.

In mathematics, the search space is often so large that you can’t simply try everything. You need some way to guide the search. But intuition alone isn’t enough either—a promising idea can be wrong, and you still have to turn it into a rigorous argument.

For an AI system, that suggests a combination of learned guidance and systematic search, ideally with a way to verify the resulting proof. And the two can reinforce each other: search can uncover successful strategies that improve the system’s future judgments. So the interesting question is how to use computation to develop better intuition, and how to use intuition to make computation more effective.

sol-6.1.text:
I think intuition and brute force play complementary roles. In mathematics, intuition helps you decide where to look: which examples to try, which intermediate statement might be useful, or which representation makes a problem easier. Brute force lets you explore possibilities and check whether those guesses actually work.

For an AI system, the interesting question is how to allocate that search. If you try every possible proof step indiscriminately, the space becomes enormous very quickly. A learned model can guide the search toward steps that seem promising, while a formal verifier can check whether each step is valid. So you have this interaction between proposing and checking.

And I wouldn’t draw too sharp a boundary between the two. What looks like intuition can reflect patterns learned from many examples, and search can uncover patterns that improve future intuition. The goal is to make exploration more productive, while keeping the standard of correctness rigorous.
